title: GPX Sequential Distance Checker: Running Totals
description: Compute cumulative distance through a GPX file's points in order with the GPX Sequential Distance Checker — distance at every point. Free, local.
summary_sentence: For example, the worked park loop's running totals read 0, 0.66, 1.41 and 2.06 kilometres at its four points — so the bench at the third point is 1.41 km in, not 'somewhere in the middle'.
quick_answer: The GPX Sequential Distance Checker walks a GPX file's points in document order and computes the cumulative distance at each one — the running total from the start. Load the file locally and read distance-at-point values — where the 5 km mark falls and how far in the viewpoint is.

body.t: Race marshals, water stations and photo points are placed by distance-along. The running total finds the coordinate nearest any target distance — splits knowledge the
Your watch claims the 5 km split at a certain corner. The cumulative table verifies or indicts the claim point by point.
A suspicious jump in the running total (0.4 km in one step) exposes a recording gap or a teleporting fix at an exact point in the sequence.
Coaches carve routes into segments by distance. The cumulative column is the carving knife.

Points A→B→C→D with hops 0.656, 0.749, 0.656 km give cumulative 0, 0.656, 1.405, 2.062 km. Each row is the previous row plus one hop — trivial arithmetic whose value is entirely in having every row, not just the last.

Cumulative totals that leap (say 8.2 → 11.9 km in one step across a tunnel) mark where recording slept. The leap is data: it tells you the file interpolated nothing and the device saw nothing for 3.7 km of road.

popular_table.note: Cumulative distance follows the recorded path in document order — waypoints and later segments enter in the file's own sequence, which is why 'document order' is in this tool's definition.

faq: Document order — why does it matter?

GPX files can hold points in any stored sequence; cumulative distance trusts the file's order as the journey's order. A shuffled file yields shuffled totals — garbage order in, gospel-looking numbers out, so check plausibility.

Within a segment, hops accumulate normally. Across a recording gap, the hop from the last point before to the first after is counted as recorded geometry — or flagged by its size, as the gap example shows.
The checker follows the file's sequence through its elements. For per-track totals, split the file or read each track's rows in its own block.
Great-circle hops between consecutive points (haversine on the WGS84 sphere), the same engine as the route-stats sum — intermediate rows and total can never disagree.
Can I find the point nearest 10 km?
Yes — scan the cumulative column for the crossing row; the point beside it is the 10 km mark to within one hop's precision.
Horizontal distance is the convention; slope distance would inflate totals by the terrain's steepness and matches nobody's signage.
